analysis.one_liner: Extends Do Not Call protections to cell phones and lets consumers sue after a single unwanted robocall.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate committee where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Current Do Not Call rules only cover people's home phone lines, and a caller generally has to make more than one unwanted call in a year before a consumer can sue. This bill would remove the 'residential' limitation so every telephone subscriber — including cell phone users — is covered, make a single unwanted call actionable, and let consumers recover the full statutory penalty instead of a reduced one. It would also require the Federal Communications Commission to rewrite its rules within 270 days to carry this out.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a phone, especially cell phone users who today fall outside the Do Not Call registry's core protections. People plagued by telemarketing and scam robocalls would gain a clearer legal right to sue after a single unwanted call, with the full statutory penalty available, which makes small claims worth pursuing and gives lawyers a reason to take them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All phone users, including cell phones

how_it_helps.text: Strikes 'residential' from the Do Not Call provisions so the rules cover all telephone subscribers, not just home landlines [S2].
Changes the private right of action so a single call by an entity within a 12-month period can support a lawsuit, instead of requiring more than one call [S2].
Removes the 'up to' qualifier on statutory damages, so courts could no longer reduce awards below the statutory amount [S2].
Directs the FCC to revise its Do Not Call regulations within 270 days of enactment to implement these changes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketers, robocall operations, and the businesses that hire them would face exposure to lawsuits after any single call to a registered number, including cell phones, and could no longer rely on reduced damage awards. Businesses that rely on outbound calling for sales would bear higher compliance and litigation costs, some of which could be passed along in prices.

drawbacks.text: Extending liability to a single call, with damages that can no longer be reduced, could expose legitimate businesses to costly suits over one mistaken call to a registered number [S2].
The bill was introduced late in a Congress with no Republican cosponsors and no committee action, so its costs and enforcement mechanics were never examined in a hearing [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Unwanted and scam robocalls are a persistent consumer nuisance and a common channel for fraud, and the bill would meaningfully strengthen the main legal tool consumers have against them. The trade-off is real: strict single-call liability with no reduced awards could hit small businesses for honest mistakes, and the bill never went through a hearing where that balance could be examined.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on March 20, 2024, with eight original cosponsors [S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S1].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the action history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telemarketers and robocall operators are better off: the narrower, residential-only rules with a multi-call threshold for lawsuits remain in place, and consumers keep receiving calls they have no practical way to sue over.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to expand Do Not Call coverage and the private right of action

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced beyond a committee referral.

industries.note: The bill would let any phone subscriber — not just landline households — sue after a single unwanted call, with damages that could no longer be reduced below the statutory amount. That dramatically expands litigation exposure for an industry that profits by placing high volumes of outbound calls, including calls that reach cell phones today without triggering Do Not Call protections.

industries.industry: Businesses that rely on outbound sales calling
industries.note: Retailers, lead generators, and debt collectors that hire call centers would face new single-call liability if a call reaches a registered number. Some legitimate callers would absorb costs from suits over mistakes, though the same rules are what shield the public from unwanted calls.
